speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: You're able to get information at a very granular level. So I'm curious to know how you're able to get the taste of a person based on their camera roll.

speaker: Marissa Mayer
text: From the photos I took of fun ski trips, it could figure out my mother's favorite ski brand, her ski style, where she was, and probably the appropriate ski length.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: We've seen the examples of Amazon shutting down access from agents, but we're also seeing Walmart, and you're a board member there, create a protocol to let agents sign up as an agent instead of a human. So I'm curious to know your take on this agentic e-commerce.

speaker: Marissa Mayer
text: The problem is that they're kind of like people, but they have this always-on, superhuman productivity level. That just means they are, in fact, slightly different. So I think having a protocol for them to interact with commerce websites, so they're not constantly crawling and scraping and trying to get prices, and they can do this in a way that's more metered and less wasteful of resources, is really the right idea.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: How would you define success now as a startup founder for you? Introduction

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Hey, this is Carlos, CEO at Product School and your host on The Product Podcast. My guest today is Marissa Mayer: Google's first woman engineer, employee number 20, then VP of Search, then CEO of Yahoo for five years. She also started the APM program at Google, which is the reason Product School exists today. She's a founder again. Her company, Dazzle, just launched, and it's a personal assistant that learns everything about you from your camera roll. Here are the things we'll cover: 40% of your photos are not memories, they're tasks; how it picked her mother's ski length from vacation photos; first task done in 45 seconds, no connectors, no setup; why her agents never impersonate you, they act on your behalf; and ten engineers shipping like a hundred. Let's get into it. [Sponsor]  AI helps us generate ideas, draft plans, and spin up work in minutes. But faster doesn't necessarily mean better. When everyone has their own AI tools, their own outputs, and their own context, you get fragmentation: fractured version control, scattered review processes, decisions happening in parallel, not in concert. Rebuilding context between people and platforms costs you time and momentum. That's where Mural comes in. Mural gives teams a shared visual canvas to bring work together. You can generate structured starting points right on the canvas instead of moving outputs between tools, keep all of your context in one place, and compatible AI agents can contribute alongside the team, bringing in context from the tools they already know. The future of work is still human. Learn more at mural.co. The Woman Behind the APM Program

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Welcome to The Product Podcast, Marissa.

speaker: Marissa Mayer
text: Thank you very much for having me. I'm excited to be here.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I thought you didn't need an intro, but then I talked to a couple of Gen Z employees at my company. I told them, "Hey guys, Marissa Mayer is coming on the pod," and they were like, "Who?" You don't understand, you are the main source of inspiration behind my company. You started the Associate Product Manager program at Google, and in a way that inspired me to start Product School as the first associate product manager program outside of Google.

speaker: Marissa Mayer
text: Well, the Associate Product Manager program is amazing, and it really is defined by the people in it. I'm excited to hear about the work you're doing, because I just think product thinking and product management are so important, and they're also evolving so much with AI.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: For the rest of the Gen Zers who might not know who you are: you joined Google as one of the first 20 employees, as a software engineer.

speaker: Marissa Mayer
text: I was Google's first woman software engineer. I interviewed when there were just seven people there, and started in the first 20 or so. I stayed there as a software engineer, then product manager, became director of consumer products, then vice president of Search and User Experience. And in the end I was vice president of Maps, Local, and Contextual Search, which eventually became Google Assistant. Then I went to Yahoo. I was CEO there for five years, and since then I've been doing startups. I had a startup, Sunshine, and now my second startup, Dazzle, which bought my first startup. Sunshine has just recently launched. So, harkening back to the days of Google Now and Google Assistant, we're building a personal assistant using AI. Why Go From Big Tech Executive to Founder Again

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: We're going to talk about all things with your new startup. But the first question I had is, what made you consider becoming a startup founder after having such an incredible career as a big tech executive?

speaker: Marissa Mayer
text: I've discovered that I just love all phases of companies. I like small, single digits, every order of magnitude: single digits, tens, hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands. I like being an IC, I like being a manager, and I love all phases of companies: hypergrowth, turnarounds. So I was inspired to try to build something. In my career, I've been lucky to be surrounded by amazing founders: Larry, Sergey, Filo and Yang at Yahoo, and many others, companies we've acquired, teams inside companies. So I really wanted to start something, and I'm very passionate about consumer tech. My career has been in consumer technology. So I wanted to start a company to see if I could have an impact on the world the same way I'd had the opportunity to at Google and Yahoo. What Is Dazzle?

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: So tell me more. What is Dazzle?

speaker: Marissa Mayer
text: Dazzle is a personal assistant that learns from your photos. We use your camera roll. We ask for permission. You can give us full access, select access, or no photos at all. And the more photos we have, the better we work. What we do is look at your historical photos, your past photos, to understand your tastes, your lifestyle, important people and places. We do that at a pretty granular level, I'll come back to that later. And the other thing we do is look at the photos you took today, to try to make your camera button a "get it done" button. If you need to buy something, fix something, book something, add it to your calendar, take notes off a whiteboard, you just snap a picture of it and Dazzle figures out what your intention is. We ask the question, "Why did you, Carlos, take this picture today?" And then we try to help you get it done. So we basically form a to-do list, but we call it a "get it done" list, because it's a to-do list that does itself with AI agents. 40% of Your Camera Roll Is Tasks, Not Memories

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: In one of the conversations we had before this, you mentioned that about 40% of camera roll photos are actually tasks, not memories.

speaker: Marissa Mayer
text: Yeah, that's the transition point from Sunshine to Dazzle. At Sunshine, we were doing various utility applications, one of which was photo sharing, and we had built a really excellent share-worthy model: when was it likely that a photo was worthy of being shared? When we were looking at precision and recall, we realized that only about 60% of the camera roll, even after you remove blurry photos or near-duplicates, was actually passing our share-worthy model. So that begs the question, what's the other 40%? The other 40% is generally things you need to get done, things you need to remember, things you need to coordinate with someone else. So we thought, well, if we have an AI agent on the camera roll waiting for you to take a picture, it can say, "Okay, if it's just a happy memory, I'll let it go, I might try to glean some information from it for the future, but if it's something you might need help with to get done, it can swing into action and offer to do those actions." Getting the Taste of a Person From Their Photos

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: You mentioned you're able to get information at a very granular level. So I'm curious how you're able to get the taste of a person based on their camera roll.

speaker: Marissa Mayer
text: Photos are the richest source of personal information available, with the lowest friction. Some examples of things we've done: just a few weeks ago, we had a user, we were doing a session here to understand how people use Dazzle, and she said she was a prolific reader, but she had a list of books she needed for book club that she hadn't bought, because she felt like she had some already. So she said, "To use Dazzle, should I just go and take pictures of all my bookshelves?" And I said, "Maybe, but let's do something else first. Why don't you just give Dazzle the reading list and see what it does?" She said, "How will that work?" And I said, "Let's just see if it does." Sure enough, she gave it to Dazzle, and Dazzle came back and said, "Actually, you do have this book, and you don't have these other two books, but you do have books by the same author." The principle is: unless your bookshelves are in the closet, when you take a picture in your living room of family or friends or cute kids, we're also getting all that information in the background. Dazzle knows, for example, all the appliances in my house, makes, model numbers, everything, because it's all in the background of my photos, just like it knew what was on this user's bookshelves at a really granular level. Another example, early in our prototyping phase: my mother wanted some new skis last ski season. It was right after we'd gotten kind of up and running. So I said, "My mom would like new skis." And Dazzle came back and said, "Well, because Margaret," because it knows Margaret is my mother, but I hadn't told it that, "because Margaret is 76 years old and she often skis in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, and she usually wears Rossignol skis, these are the skis we would recommend for her." And then I even got a recommendation on length. I said, "She's thinking about the 164 versus the 157." And it said, "Well, because Jackson Hole is very steep, and because she's a little bit on the older side, shorter skis will be easier to maneuver." I said, "My mother's pushing back, because she says her friends all have skis that are the 160-centimeter length." And it said, "Yes, but in the photos, your mother is usually shorter and slighter than her friends, and therefore needs a shorter ski." Which is really, I mean, it's incredible that from the photos I took of fun ski trips, it could figure out my mother's favorite ski brand, her ski style, where she was, and probably even the appropriate ski length. So, really amazing things like that. Keeping a Moat in Fast-Moving AI

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: It's an amazing angle. One of the things that comes to mind about product is that we also have examples of companies that saw something happen and then copied it. In social media, Instagram copied Stories from Snapchat. Now we're seeing the same with AI meeting note-takers, Granola and others copying each other all the time. So how are you thinking about keeping your moat?

speaker: Marissa Mayer
text: In the fast-moving world of AI, there isn't much of a moat. We do have a lot of intellectual property. We thought we created some really amazing technology here, and we have patents pending on what I think will be foundational patents in terms of how to use images to help LLMs and AI understand context for a person. We were thoughtful about really wanting to protect that intellectual property, because we think it's unique. But there are also things that are obvious to those skilled in the art. There's now a whole crop of personal AI systems that have launched, and it was interesting: many of them launched invite-only, as we did. Many of them launched on iMessage, which we've been working on since the spring. So it's interesting to see some of the ideas we were building validated now by other competitors. Though the photos piece does remain unique. Why Consumer AI

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Your product is focused on consumer applications, not business context.

speaker: Marissa Mayer
text: That's right. I think consumer AI is going to be much larger. I've been fascinated by AI since my college days, and I've always worked in consumer. When we were pitching Dazzle last year to VCs, one of the things I learned was that today only about 6% of investment in AI goes to consumer, yet the consumer market is expected to be twice the size of the enterprise market by 2030. So it points to the fact that there's a big opportunity there. It also means I love to build for consumers, because I think it's easier for me to adopt that consumer mindset, that user mindset, to really build something they want that works for them. But it presents unique challenges. One of the things we've been most fixated on at Dazzle is how quickly we can get someone who isn't tech-savvy up and doing their first task with an AI agent. When you look at many of the other tools out there, you have to do so much setup, connectors, everything else, and you really have to understand the technology to do it. It's a point of pride that at Dazzle, from the moment you first open the app to actually doing your first task on your "get it done" list, it's usually 45 seconds or less. I think that's remarkable. I grew up in the Midwest, and the friends I've tested the product with just can't believe it. They're like, "It doesn't even feel like there's a lot of setup. It doesn't feel like you're using an AI agent. It really just feels much more fluid and natural, and it's really fast." I think that's a key element for consumers. Staying Competitive Against the Giants

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I agree. I think the reason we're leading through this supercycle with AI assistants now is because, finally, regular consumers can use these capabilities within their current apps, like WhatsApp and iMessage. You don't need to download anything if you don't want to, and you don't need to worry about connectors. At the same time, Marissa, I see that you raised around $8 million, and you have a nimble team, and you're up against a lot of well-funded players. I'm sure OpenAI and Claude are also going to come up with their own solutions for this. So how are you thinking about staying competitive, given that they can subsidize this product for a very long time?

speaker: Marissa Mayer
text: Dazzle is currently free as well, so we're also subsidizing. But for us, we're really focused on our early users: what do they like about the product? The feedback has been very strong. The engagement has been incredible, as has the retention. These products that meet users' needs are very sticky. So we need more distribution, and we're working on that. We also need to keep evolving with new features, because it's a quickly evolving space. But we're really focused right now on the users and on building the best product, while keeping an eye on how we get this in the hands of as many people as possible, and keeping it really simple, really easy to set up and use. In my view, there's a shockingly small number of people who are really using AI at all, let alone to its fullest capabilities. The gap between what people know AI can do is getting ever wider, between the people who use AI and the people who don't. That's one of the things Dazzle is designed to address: how do we take people who are maybe skeptical of AI, hesitant to use AI, and help them in their personal lives, outside of the work context, in a way that's purely a help? It's trying to give you the gift of time. The Human Concierge and Agentic Commerce

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Speaking of monetization, you mentioned the example with your mom being recommended a pair of skis. I saw that you also have a human concierge team that, in a way, acts as a human in the loop depending on what products are being recommended. So how are you thinking about the agentic e-commerce application on top of your own platform?

speaker: Marissa Mayer
text: We do use agentic commerce, and the vast majority of transactions Dazzle does go through agents. But if something is particularly expensive or particularly complicated, we route it to our human concierges for a final check. In the end, this might end up being something where we have agents checking agents. But right now, one of our investors is Sam Lessin, who previously ran a personal assistant company called Fin, and he commented to me, "You have no idea how quickly you lose a user when they're expecting red shoes and green shoes show up." And I was like, I believe it, because people are picky. When they decide to splurge or use a personal assistant to get something they really want, it needs to be right. Some of these soft goods in particular are really complicated. Last week I was trying to buy something that came in clear, mirrored, and smoke. The agent understandably got confused. We saw a low-confidence signal and we intervened, just to make sure we could actually get it right. The commerce itself is also really complicated. For Halloween, my daughter was doing a group costume, and they decided on a t-shirt that came in a two-pack, and we went to order the two-pack of t-shirts and it was sold out, not available until November 17th. There was a lot of consternation, she was really upset about it. It took me a minute to think about it, and then I was like, "Oh, maybe the black t-shirt we need is available in a different two-pack." And sure enough, while black and red was sold out until November 17th, black and light pink was available. So we bought it, got the t-shirt, no problem. But that's hard at this point. Maybe in 2027, agents are going to be able to figure that out. Sometimes you need that human intuition, that human insight, to be like, "Wait, given how this is packaged, I wonder if I can get the same product packaged a different way." And sure enough, you could. So there are things like that where, in personal assistant tasks, if you can figure out a way to make it happen, that's what you have to do. That's where our concierges are focused. Agentic Commerce and Agents Identifying as Agents

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I think the other challenge we're seeing with agents trying to do commerce is that the web is still designed for humans. We've seen the examples of Amazon shutting down access from agents, but we're also seeing Walmart, and you're a board member there, create an agentic protocol to let agents sign up as an agent instead of a human. So I'm curious to know your take on this agentic e-commerce, and agents being able to identify themselves as an agent and not just as a fake human.

speaker: Marissa Mayer
text: I think agentic e-commerce is a really good approach. Having proper protocols for agents just eliminates a lot of problems. A few months ago, I remember reading, because basically these agents come in and they look like humans, but then they behave almost like a denial-of-service attack. I remember reading one story where someone was trying to find kiss-cam footage of themselves and their boyfriend, and they sent their agent out to find it, and I think it emailed a production assistant at a local TV station 1,800 times in nine hours. So the problem is that they're kind of like people, but they have this always-on, superhuman productivity level, which just means they are, in fact, slightly different. So having a protocol for them to interact with commerce websites, so they're not constantly crawling and scraping and trying to get prices, and they can do this in a way that's more metered and less wasteful of resources, is actually a good and prudent idea. In the meantime, here at Dazzle, we have a slightly different view of how to approach this, which is that we like to do things on your behalf, as opposed to as you. What that means is our agents, both AI and human, have their own email addresses, their own phone numbers, their own credit cards, their own accounts with most of the major vendors. Therefore they're not acting as Carlos when they go to do a purchase. We've seen instances where, when AI can impersonate you and it does the wrong thing, it can cause big problems. We've heard stories about canceled flights with other assistant apps, and you'd be like, "Well, how can that even happen?" But the AI is calling the airline pretending to be you, and it has all the credentials to make that happen. I have a personal assistant, I understand that's a point of privilege and a real luxury, but she never has to impersonate me. She always calls as herself, on my behalf, not as me, and she's really effective that way. We think that, at least at this current moment of AI, is how we should approach it. When you go and buy something, it's either the AI agent buying it as the AI agent, and they have names on the accounts as such, or it's the human, and then we ultimately have you reimburse us for the cost, and we get the item shipped to you. But the way we behave in this agentic commerce model, and in an inquiry model when we're doing things like booking home repairs, is quite different. Running a Ten-Person Team That Ships Like a Hundred

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I want to switch gears for a second and talk about the magic behind the scenes, because you have a nimble team and you're working hard. First of all, what is your real involvement as CEO of the company?

speaker: Marissa Mayer
text: I'm here five or six days a week in person, working every day in person, but I love it. I have a great team, I think we have a great idea, and it's been really amazing to see how our early users respond to it. It's been really positive, so it's a lot of fun. This is my full-time gig.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: What's the secret sauce? How can a team of ten engineers and a few others really compete with the giants?

speaker: Marissa Mayer
text: One is focus. As a smaller company, we have to. It's not a luxury, it's a necessity, that we decide this is what we're going to focus on: how do we take photos and make them incredibly useful, how do we work on this task? So part of it is just making sure you're not spread too thin. But I also have to say, with the power of agentic coding, we have a team of 10 to 12 engineers and they code more like a team of 100, because each of them is running so many different agents. We generally have most people running five, ten, sometimes even more agents at any given time to get tasks done. So we're able to produce in a way that, just a few years ago, would have required many more people. Model-Agnostic by Design

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: In terms of model usage, and how you're architecting the company behind the scenes so you can focus on your competitive advantage, tell me about it.

speaker: Marissa Mayer
text: Sure. The product itself, that's part of the Dazzle product, is model-agnostic. Whenever there's a new model that comes out, we assess which task it's good for. At any given time, we usually have three or four frontier models in play. We also have a few smaller models, some classifiers and things on-device, and some models on-device, as well as others that work server-side. So we're constantly looking at how we can swap out to the best technology, how we can use whatever is highest quality and most efficient, because speed also matters for people in the product. And here at the startup, we all use AI a lot, both for coding, for strategy, planning, and for trying to analyze the data coming off our early users. It's been an invaluable tool. How Marissa Defines Success Now

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: So, Marissa, you came out of stealth recently, and the launch seems to be going well. At the same time, you achieved such a level of success in your previous life as a big tech executive that there's a big gap to fill. So as you think about the future, when you look back, how would you define success now as a startup founder?

speaker: Marissa Mayer
text: I think we want to have a meaningful, positive impact on a large number of users. Right now, I can see the green shoots, where our users really love what we're doing, and they really value the gift of time and how easy we're making it to do things. I myself find it incredibly useful. So it's fulfilling for me to see that we're really helping people. Now we need to do it at scale, and to do it at scale means we have to get more distribution, and we need to keep evolving the product, winning more and new users with new features and new capabilities. So for me, it really comes down to the positive impact on individuals' lives, and hopefully on a large number of individuals.
